questions.stem: When you analyse a Japanese text in the short response examination, what do the four elements of PACT stand for?
options: Plot, argument, character and theme
Perspective, audience, culture and text type
Purpose, argument, content and theme
Purpose, audience, context and tone
questions.explanation: PACT is purpose (why the text was written), audience (who it is for), context (where, when and in what situation) and tone (the attitude or feeling it conveys). Two are answered in English and the other two in Japanese.

questions.stem: 「みなさん、来週の土曜日に、町の公園でごみひろいをします。だれでもさんかできます。ぜひ来てください！」 What is the main purpose of this notice?
options: To thank the people who cleaned the park
To invite people to join a park clean-up
To report on a clean-up that took place
To complain about the rubbish in the park
questions.explanation: The event is in the future (来週の土曜日), anyone can take part (だれでもさんかできます), and 「ぜひ来てください」 urges readers to come. Those features point to an invitation, not a report or a complaint.

questions.stem: 「新入生のみなさん、入学おめでとう！部活を見学したい人は、四月十日までに三階の音楽室に来てね。」 Who is the audience?
options: Parents of the students starting school
New students at the school
Students who are about to graduate
Music teachers who run the school clubs
questions.explanation: 「新入生のみなさん」 addresses new students directly, and 「入学おめでとう」 congratulates them on starting school. The friendly 「来てね」 also suits fellow students rather than parents or teachers.

questions.stem: 「また電車がおくれた。これで今週三どめだ。いいかげんにしてほしい。」 Which word best describes the tone?
options: Irritated
Grateful
Anxious
Nostalgic
questions.explanation: 「また」 (again), counting the third time this week, and 「いいかげんにしてほしい」 ('I wish they'd get it together') all show irritation. Nothing suggests worry about the outcome, so anxious does not fit.

questions.stem: 「田中先生、おいそがしいところ、もうしわけありません。来週のスピーチについて、ごそうだんしたいことがございます。」 Which feature best shows that the writer is addressing someone of higher status?
options: Polite and humble expressions such as もうしわけありません and ございます
Sentence-final particles such as よ and ね that soften requests
Katakana loanwords that make the message sound up to date
Plain-form verbs that keep the message short and direct
questions.explanation: 「おいそがしいところ」, 「もうしわけありません」, 「ごそうだん」 and 「ございます」 are keigo, used upward to a teacher. よ and ね, and plain forms, would mark a casual message to a friend.

questions.stem: 「お花見のばしょとりをたのまれたので、朝六時から公園にいます。」 What is the context of this post?
options: New Year: the writer is in the park early to see the first sunrise
Spring: keeping a spot in the park for a cherry blossom party
Autumn: the writer is waiting in the park to see the leaves change colour
Summer: the writer is queuing early in the park for a fireworks festival
questions.explanation: 「お花見」 is cherry-blossom viewing in spring, and 「ばしょとり」 is saving a spot. 「たのまれた」 (passive) shows someone asked the writer to do it, which is why they are there at six in the morning.

questions.stem: A message reads 「ごめん！ねぼうしちゃった。十分おくれる！」 What does 「しちゃった」 tell you?
options: It is a command form of する, telling the reader to hurry up
It is a question form of した, asking whether the reader overslept
A casual form of してしまった, showing regret: to a close friend
It is a humble form of しました, showing respect, so it is to a teacher
questions.explanation: 「〜ちゃった」 is the spoken contraction of 「〜てしまった」, which adds regret: 'I went and overslept'. Contractions, plain forms and 「ごめん」 mark a casual message between friends.

questions.stem: 「明日のパーティー、来るよね？」 What does 「よね」 show here?
options: The speaker is giving a strong order that must be followed
The speaker is turning down an invitation politely
The speaker is checking an assumption with someone close
The speaker is formally inviting someone they have not met
questions.explanation: 「よね」 seeks confirmation of something the speaker already believes: 'You're coming, right?'. With the dropped particle and plain 「来る」, it suggests a friend.

questions.stem: A poster asks students to help at the school's summer festival. Which statement describes its context rather than its purpose?
options: It aims to persuade students to volunteer at the festival
It wants readers to sign up with their teacher by Friday
It tries to make helping at the festival sound like fun
It went up on the noticeboard a week before the festival
questions.explanation: Context is the situation: where and when the text appears and in what circumstances. The other statements are about what the poster is trying to achieve, which is its purpose.

questions.stem: 「わあ、すごい！夢みたい！」 Which word best describes the tone?
options: Delighted
Disappointed
Worried
Bored
questions.explanation: 「わあ」 and 「すごい」 are exclamations of delight, and 「夢みたい」 ('like a dream') shows the speaker can hardly believe their luck. The exclamation marks support the reading.

questions.stem: In a short Japanese text, which language feature most clearly suggests that the purpose is to persuade?
options: Place words such as 〜の前 and 〜のとなり
Invitations such as 〜ませんか and 〜ましょう
Past-tense verbs such as 〜ました and 〜でした
Counters such as 〜まい and 〜本 with numbers
questions.explanation: 「いっしょに〜しませんか」 and 「〜しましょう」 draw the reader into acting, which signals a persuasive purpose. Past-tense verbs suit a recount, and place words suit directions.

questions.stem: Which statement evaluates a text rather than simply describing it?
options: The text uses the polite です and ます style throughout
Questions to the reader make the appeal personal, so it persuades well
The writer asks the reader two questions in the middle part of the text
The text is an email written by a student to a host family
questions.explanation: Evaluation judges how well the text works and why: the questions make it personal, and so it is effective. The other statements only describe features without judging their effect.

questions.stem: Answering in Japanese, which sentence correctly says the poster was written to gather participants?
options: 「このポスターは、さんかしゃをあつめてために書かれました。」
「このポスターは、さんかしゃをあつめるために書かれました。」
「このポスターは、さんかしゃをあつめるためで書かれました。」
「このポスターは、さんかしゃをあつめるのために書かれました。」
questions.explanation: Purpose 「ために」 follows the plain form of the verb directly: 「あつめるために」. 「の」 is only used before ために after a noun (さんかしゃのために), and 「で」 or the て-form cannot stand there. 「書かれました」 is the passive, 'was written'.

questions.stem: 「このメールは、ホストファミリーにむけて書かれています。」 What does 「にむけて」 tell you?
options: Who the email is aimed at
Where the email was written
When the email was sent
Why the email was written
questions.explanation: 「〜にむけて」 means 'directed at' or 'aimed at', so it names the audience: the host family. It is a useful phrase for stating audience in a Japanese answer.

questions.stem: Asked in Japanese 「このブログのトーンはどうですか。」, which answer is in a full sentence, as the task requires?
options: 「とても明るいブログ」
「このブログのトーンは明るくて、楽しそうです。」
「明るい。楽しそう。」
「明るくて楽しいトーン」
questions.explanation: Only the first answer has a subject (このブログのトーンは) and a complete predicate (明るくて、楽しそうです). The others are fragments, which do not meet the requirement to respond in full sentences.

questions.stem: In the short response examination, which of these is allowed?
options: Using a dictionary
Hearing the audio with English subtitles
Typing your answers on a computer
Replaying the audio as often as you like
questions.explanation: Dictionaries may be used in the short response examination. Audio stimulus has no English subtitles and is played up to three times, and responses must be handwritten.

questions.stem: How do the short response and extended response examinations differ on dictionaries?
options: Allowed in the extended response, not in the short response
Allowed in both examinations
Allowed in neither examination
Allowed in the short response, not in the extended response
questions.explanation: Students may use dictionaries when analysing texts in the short response examination, but not in the extended response. The external examination also allows no dictionaries.

questions.stem: The written extended response task gives three bullet points in Japanese. What should your response do?
options: Address all three focuses within one text
Choose the one focus you know the most about
Answer each focus briefly in English first
Write a separate short text for each focus
questions.explanation: The task requires one written response that discusses three different focuses, so each bullet point must be covered within the single text type set, such as a blog or a letter.

questions.stem: During the extended response you cannot remember the kanji for a word. What should you do?
options: Write the word in English
Leave a blank in its place
Write the word in hiragana
Write the word in romaji
questions.explanation: Romaji may not be used in responses for assessment, so write the word in kana. Hiragana keeps the Japanese intact, while English or a gap loses the meaning.

questions.stem: In vertical writing (たてがき) on げんこうようし, where does a small 「っ」 go?
options: In the same square as the kana before it
In its own square, centred and full size
In the margin beside the line of text
In its own square, towards the top right
questions.explanation: Small kana such as っ, ゃ, ゅ and ょ take a square of their own. In vertical writing they sit in the upper right of that square, so they read as small.

questions.stem: In vertical writing on げんこうようし, how is the long vowel mark 「ー」 written?
options: As a small 「あ」
It is left out
As a vertical line
As a horizontal line
questions.explanation: In たてがき the long vowel mark turns with the text and is written as a vertical stroke. In horizontal writing (よこがき) it is a horizontal line.

questions.stem: On horizontal げんこうようし, how is a two-digit number such as 25 usually written?
options: Each digit takes its own square
The number goes in the margin
The number takes three squares
Both digits share one square
questions.explanation: In よこがき, Arabic numerals are written two to a square, so 25 fills one square. Writing each digit in its own square is a common slip that wastes space.

questions.stem: Which sentence would typically end a blog post and invite readers to respond?
options: 「来週の月曜日までにへんじをください。」
「みなさんはどう思いますか。コメントしてくださいね。」
「ごせいちょう、ありがとうございました。」
「では、お体に気をつけてください。けいぐ」
questions.explanation: A blog often closes by asking readers' views and inviting comments. 「ごせいちょう」 ends a speech, 「けいぐ」 closes a formal letter, and a reply deadline suits an email.

questions.stem: Which is most typical of a text message to a friend?
options: 「今どこ？駅の前で待ってるね。」
「はいけい、春になりました。」
「本日はおいそがしいところ、ありがとうございます。」
「このもんだいについて考えてみたい。」
questions.explanation: Text messages are short and casual, with plain forms, dropped particles and contractions such as 「待ってる」. 「はいけい」 opens a formal letter, 「本日は」 is formal speech, and the last sounds like an essay.

questions.stem: Which opening would best draw in the audience of a speech?
options: 「みなさんは、日本のアニメを見たことがありますか。」
「私は、日本のアニメについて書きました。」
「これで、私の話を終わります。」
「アニメのことは、よく知りません。」
questions.explanation: A question to the audience, here with 「〜たことがありますか」, involves listeners from the start. 「書きました」 belongs to written work, and 「これで〜終わります」 ends a speech.

questions.stem: Which sentence proposes a future course of action?
options: 「これからは、毎日三十分日本語のドラマを見るようにしようと思います。」
「その時、私はとてもはずかしかったです。」
「時間がなかったので、バスに乗りました。」
「先月、日本へ行きました。」
questions.explanation: 「これからは」 (from now on) with 「〜ようにしようと思います」 (I intend to make a point of) proposes what the writer will do. The others recall a feeling, explain a past action and report an event.

questions.stem: Which sentence reflects on an experience rather than just reporting it?
options: 「東京では、えいがを見たり、買い物をしたりしました。」
「今思うと、あのしっぱいのおかげで、人に聞くことのたいせつさが分かりました。」
「先週、友達と東京へ行って、電車に乗りまちがえました。」
「東京の電車はとても多くて、駅もとても大きいです。」
questions.explanation: 「今思うと」 (looking back now) and 「〜のおかげで〜が分かりました」 show what the writer learned from the mistake: reflection. The other sentences report what happened or describe Tokyo.

questions.stem: Which sentence explains the writer's behaviour?
options: 「ホームステイの家族は、とてもやさしかったです。」
「ホームステイは、日本で三週間でした。」
「みなさんも、ぜひホームステイをしてみてください。」
「日本語が上手になりたかったので、ホームステイをすることにしました。」
questions.explanation: 「〜たかったので」 gives the reason (wanting to improve) and 「〜ことにしました」 the decision it led to, so the sentence explains why the writer acted. The last sentence recommends, and the others describe.

questions.stem: In the conversation, the teacher asks a question you didn't expect. Which phrase gives you a moment to think naturally?
options: 「英語でこたえてもいいですか。」
「そのしつもんは、ちょっと…。」
「そうですね…。むずかしいしつもんですが、」
「わかりません。つぎ、おねがいします。」
questions.explanation: 「そうですね…」 is a natural filler, and acknowledging the question is hard buys time before answering. Refusing, skipping or switching to English ends the exchange instead of sustaining it.

questions.stem: The teacher uses a word you don't know. Which question asks what it means?
options: 「すみません、もう少しゆっくり話していただけませんか。」
「すみません、そのことばは何語ですか。」
「すみません、もう時間ですか。」
「すみません、今のことばは、どういう意味ですか。」
questions.explanation: 「どういう意味ですか」 asks for the meaning, a strategy for keeping the conversation going. Asking the teacher to slow down helps with speed, not with an unknown word.

questions.stem: Asked 「日本のドラマが好きですか。」, which answer best sustains the conversation?
options: 「ドラマですか。ええと、ドラマはドラマですね。」
「はい、とくにれんあいドラマが好きです。先生はどうですか。」
「はい、好きです。日本のドラマは日本で作られています。」
「はい、好きです。でも、どうしてそれを聞くんですか。」
questions.explanation: The best answer adds a detail (とくにれんあいドラマ) and turns the question back to the teacher, keeping the exchange going. Stating an obvious fact or challenging the question does neither.

questions.stem: In the spoken part of the extended response, what is the unseen stimulus used for?
options: A passage to translate into English during planning
A topic to summarise in a written paragraph first
A springboard for a talk with unseen questions
A text to read aloud word for word to the teacher
questions.explanation: The short visual or written stimulus starts the conversation, which then moves through unseen, open-ended questions. Students may make notes in planning time but do not read it aloud or translate it.
